turns.en: To learn more, visit psum.vc. Walter, I've been looking forward to this for many, many months. We were introduced through Jeremy Stern, who runs Colossus, who I know credits you with a lot of his skill in writing and thinking about the world.
turns.zh: 更多内容请访问 psum.vc。Walter，这场对话我盼了好多好多个月了。我们是通过 Jeremy Stern 认识的，他主理 Colossus，我知道他把自己的写作功底和对世界的思考很大程度上归功于你。

turns.en: I've been so excited to do this with you. We've got such a wide range of topics that I thought it would be appropriate to begin by having you frame your view of America in the world today.
turns.zh: 能和你做这期节目我特别兴奋。我们话题非常广，所以我想，开场先请你搭建一下你今天对美国在世界中位置的整体看法，可能比较合适。

turns.en: In very, very broad strokes, you've written a lot about how and why the UK and then us as the successor in America have won the last several hundred years of global affairs.
turns.zh: 在非常、非常宏观的层面上，你写了很多，讲英国、然后作为继承者的美国，是如何、以及为何赢下了过去几百年的全球事务。

turns.en: I'd love you to talk about the sweep of that winning, how you conceive of us and our role in the world today. It's a really interesting time because on the one hand, the Pax Americana that we developed after 1945 and then refurbished in 1990 at the end of the Cold War is really in crisis.
turns.zh: 我很想听你讲讲这场胜利的宏大脉络，你怎么看我们自己、以及我们在当今世界中的角色。这真是个有意思的时代，因为一方面，我们在 1945 年之后建立、又在 1990 年冷战结束时修缮的美国治世（Pax Americana），确实正处于危机之中。

turns.en: But if you step back a little bit, American power is not in crisis. The networks that we built up, the way of dealing with the world, the institutionalized relations with Europe and so on, those are all burning or crumbling.
turns.zh: 但稍微往后退一步看，美国的权力本身并不处于危机。我们建立的那些网络、与世界打交道的方式、与欧洲的制度化关系等等，这些都在燃烧或者崩塌。

turns.en: But the United States as a power, it seems to me, is if anything, thanks to the information revolution and sort of this extraordinary raises in productivity that I believe we have experienced and are about to experience, I think we're still charging ahead.
turns.zh: 但美国作为一个大国，在我看来，如果说有什么的话，得益于信息革命、以及我相信我们已经经历、并即将经历的那种种非凡的生产力提升，我觉得我们仍然在一路向前冲。

turns.en: It's this odd picture of a dynamic country and a collapsing world system. The Trump presidency has kind of exaggerated a lot of the disruption.
turns.zh: 这是一幅奇特的图景：一个国家充满活力，一个世界体系却在坍塌。特朗普的总统任期可以说放大了很多这种动荡。

turns.en: I'm optimistic about America's position medium to long term. I do think we're in rough waters right now. What do you mean by collapsing world system?
turns.zh: 中长期看，我对美国的地位是乐观的，但我确实觉得我们现在身处险滩。你说的『正在坍塌的世界体系』是什么意思？

turns.en: While you think about the World Trade Organization, we used to have this rules-based system for trade. Now your tariff is more or less what President Trump wakes up in the morning and thinks it should be.
turns.zh: 想想世界贸易组织（WTO）就知道了，我们过去有一套基于规则的贸易体系。现在关税是多少，差不多就是特朗普总统早上醒来觉得应该是多少就是多少。

turns.en: As a country, we exercised more of our power through institutions, the NATO Alliance, the UN even at times, and we're not doing that. Since World War II, it's been sort of a principle of American foreign policy that we want to be steady, predictable.
turns.zh: 作为一个国家，我们过去更多是通过制度来行使权力——北约同盟、有时候甚至包括联合国——而现在我们不这么做了。二战以来，美国外交政策有一条基本原则：我们要沉稳、可预测。

turns.en: You want everybody to know where America's red lines are. You want everybody to be able to relive. We made a commitment in 1955, unless we announced with great fanfare that it's changing, it's still there.
turns.zh: 你希望所有人都知道美国的红线在哪里，希望所有人都能以此为凭。我们 1955 年许下的承诺，除非我们高调宣布它变了，否则它就还在。

turns.en: So we were trying to provide this bedrock of solidity in the world, and we're obviously not trying to do that anymore. For President Trump, I think he believes he maximizes his advantages by being completely unpredictable and also crossing a lot of lines so that past presidents probably would not have said things like, okay, if you don't raise your defense budget, we're going to double your tariffs or something of that kind and try to solve problems through channels.
turns.zh: 所以我们过去是想给世界提供一种坚实的地基，而现在显然不想这么干了。对特朗普总统，我认为他相信，彻底让人捉摸不透、并且大量越过界线，能把他的优势最大化。换作过去的总统，大概不会说出『你不提高国防预算，我就把你的关税翻一倍』这类话，他们过去会尝试通过既有渠道解决问题。

turns.en: Trump would make the argument that didn't work, and so he's now completely trashing the institutional networks that for a very long time were the vessels of American power, and I think he's doing it in a way that's going to be very hard for his successors to rebuild.
turns.zh: 特朗普会论证说那套行不通，所以他现在把那些长期以来作为美国权力载体的制度网络砸了个稀碎，而且我认为他砸的方式，会让他的继任者很难再重建起来。

turns.en: How would you teach someone else his method? You've written a lot about this. I'm very curious how you framed it. He's an interesting president, no doubt, whether you're for or against what he's been doing.
turns.zh: 你会怎么把他这套方法教给别人？你写了很多这方面的东西，我很好奇你是怎么提炼的。无论赞成还是反对他正在做的事，他无疑是一位耐人寻味的总统。

turns.en: How would you teach his method to somebody that was curious to learn how he operates? So distinctive. He really is a genius. He's discovered, I think, one of the secrets of power in the contemporary world, which is he's managed to turn fame into power, drama into power, and to do it in ways that leave him completely free to act.
turns.zh: 如果要教一个好奇他如何运作的人，你会怎么教他的方法？太独特了。他真的是个天才。我想他发现了当代世界权力的一个秘密：他把名声变成了权力，把戏剧性变成了权力，而且他做得让自己完全拥有行动的自由。

turns.en: If you lie enough, the marginal cost of your 10,000th lie is nothing. While the marginal law of your first, second, or third, the marginal cost is very high.
turns.zh: 谎话撒得够多，第一万个谎言的边际成本就几乎为零；而第一、第二、第三个谎言，边际成本却高得惊人。

turns.en: All of the normal constraints on political figures, reputation, and so on, he does not pay. In some ways, I think President Clinton first discovered that shame only matters if you let it.
turns.zh: 政客身上那些常规约束——名声等等——他一概不买账。某种程度上，我觉得克林顿总统第一个发现了：羞耻心只有当你在乎它的时候才有用。

turns.en: Shame is an emotion that exists in other people's minds. A lot of people thought when the Monica Lewinsky thing came out he would have no choice but to resign.
turns.zh: 羞耻是存在于别人脑子里的一种情绪。当初 Monica Lewinsky 事件曝光时，很多人觉得他除了辞职别无选择。

turns.en: He was so overwhelming, so dreadful. He basically realized, no, if you just keep putting one foot in front of the other, you just pass through.
turns.zh: 那阵势那么排山倒海、那么可怕。但他基本上悟到了：不对，你只要一步接一步往前走，就能穿过去了。

turns.en: The dogs will bark, but the caravan will move on. Trump has deployed that concept on an industrial scale. Can you talk about this notion of speech and spectacle?
turns.zh: 犬吠随它犬吠，商队照常前行。特朗普把这一理念用到了工业化的规模。你能讲讲『言辞与奇观』（speech and spectacle）这个说法吗？

turns.en: Can you say more just about what you mean there? The Donald Trump show is the most compelling entertainment, infotainment spectacle that humanity has ever seen.
turns.zh: 你再展开说说你指的是什么？『Donald Trump 秀』是人类见过的最抓人的娱乐、资讯娱乐奇观。

turns.en: Since the dawn of time, no living human being has occupied the amount of bandwidth of the human race that Donald Trump does. Now, we can say, well, global media and so on, but it's very hard to think ever of a single ruler who just dominated everything.
turns.zh: 自有人类以来，没有任何一个活着的人像 Donald Trump 这样占据了全人类这么多的带宽。你可以说，这是因为全球媒体什么的，但很难想象历史上哪个统治者能这样支配一切。

turns.en: Anywhere you go in the world today, I don't care where it is, what you hear is Trump, Trump, Trump, Trump, Trump. Some people hate Trump. Some people love Trump.
turns.zh: 今天你到世界上任何地方，不管哪儿，听到的都是 Trump、Trump、Trump、Trump、Trump。有人恨 Trump，有人爱 Trump。

turns.en: Some people laugh at Trump. Some people are astonished by Trump. Some people spend their lives thinking about their contempt for Trump, but he remains the center of everything.
turns.zh: 有人嘲笑 Trump，有人被 Trump 震惊，有人终其一生都在咀嚼自己对 Trump 的蔑视——但他始终是一切的中心。

turns.en: And he sees that as the key to his unique power. A lot of people thought that when he lost in 2020, he would go away, that that was it. He was just about as dominant out of office as he had been in office.
turns.zh: 而他把这看作自己独特权力的关键。很多人以为 2020 年他败选之后他就会消失，故事就完了。结果他下野时的支配力，和在任时几乎不相上下。

turns.en: At what he does, he is as good as Napoleon was at what he did. I observed that Napoleon also lost at Waterloo and ended in exile, so this is no guarantee that it will be what Trump would consider a happy ending to the whole spectacle.
turns.zh: 在他做的事情上，他就像当年拿破仑之于他做的事情一样登峰造极。不过我也说了一句：拿破仑也在 Waterloo 输了，最后流亡收场，所以并不保证这整场奇观会有一个在 Trump 看来圆满的结局。

turns.en: But he is a major historic figure who has developed a new understanding of how power works in an era of mass communications and social media, and the rest of us are just trying to deal with it.
turns.zh: 但他无疑是一位重量级的历史人物，他对大众传播和社交媒体时代权力如何运作形成了新的理解，而我们其他人不过是在设法应对罢了。

turns.en: How do you think the world is or will be the most different because of his role in it? Well, I think he has vastly accelerated the disintegration of the post-World War II slash post-Cole War structures.
turns.zh: 因为他的存在，世界最大的不同——现在或将来——会是什么？嗯，我认为他大大加速了二战后、也就是冷战后这套结构的瓦解。

turns.en: They're not going to be the same. He's not the only one who's done this, but I think we're entering an era of much more personal and much less bureaucratic politics.
turns.zh: 它们不会再是原来的样子了。做这件事的不止他一个，但我认为我们正在进入一个更个人化、更少官僚政治的时代。

turns.en: That is, I think for a long time in the 20th century, people got into the habit of thinking one person rule or a central figure should be downgraded and we should be run by institutions and bureaucrats and or committees.
turns.zh: 我是说，20 世纪有很长时间，人们养成了一种习惯性的想法：一个人统治、一个核心人物，这种东西应该被贬低，我们应该由机构、官僚、或者委员会来治理。

turns.en: I think that one of the impacts of the internet is that people want to be ruled by people again, so that in India you see a Modi. We saw Abe in Japan, Beebe in Israel and Erdogan in Turkey and Trump in the United States.
turns.zh: 我觉得互联网的影响之一，就是人们又想被人——一个活生生的强人——来统治了。所以你在印度看到 Modi，在日本看到过 Abe，在以色列看到 Bibi，在土耳其看到 Erdogan，在美国看到 Trump。

turns.en: Trump is the greatest of these, the most globally impactful of this new wave of Putin, Xi Jinping. We're back to an era of personal politics.
turns.zh: Trump 是其中最厉害的一个，是这新一波——和 Putin、Xi Jinping 一道——里全球影响力最大的。我们回到了个人政治的时代。

turns.en: If you think about the broader, longer arc of dominance or power leading up to this moment, I love the historical context you're an amazing historian.
turns.zh: 如果我们把时间拉长、看更宽的权力与主导地位的弧线——一路走到今天——我很喜欢你的历史视角。你是一位了不起的历史学家。

turns.en: Talk about why, whether it's maritime dominance or other major reasons, that you think the UK and America up until, let's say, the end of the Cold War or something had such an incredible run.
turns.zh: 讲讲为什么吧——无论是海权主导还是其他关键原因——为什么你认为英国和美国一直到，比如说，冷战结束，都有那么一段不可思议的连胜。

turns.en: Let's just start with the US-China rivalry today. What you see is the two sides. One is a land-based continental empire, China, which believes that it can match the technological and therefore military strength of the other power without all that political liberalism and messy democracy.
turns.zh: 就从今天的中美竞争说起吧。你会看到两方：一方是陆权的大陆帝国——China——它相信自己能够匹敌另一方在技术上、进而在军事上的实力，而不需要那些政治自由主义和乱糟糟的民主。

turns.en: Great idea. The first, I think, ruler in modern times to really embrace that was Louis XIV, who thought that his technocratic government of the experts in France could beat those pesky English with all of that ridiculous, you know, every 20 years they kill the king or kick him out or what, who knows what they do.
turns.zh: 好主意。我想现代第一个真正拥抱这套想法的统治者，是 Louis XIV，他觉得法国这套专家治国的技术官僚政府，能打败那些烦人的 English——English 那套太荒唐了：每二十年就把国王杀掉或者赶走，鬼知道他们在干什么。

turns.en: But it's utterly chaotic. The French idea was we can do that with a strong centralized system. From the time of Louis XIV right up until now, you could sort of argue the dominant theme of global power politics has been this rise of this English-speaking maritime commercial liberal order and then it's being contested successively by a series of great power continental states, France under Louis XIV, again with Napoleon, Germany, Prussian World War I and
turns.zh: 但那看起来 utterly chaotic。法国的想法是：我们用一个强大的中央集权体制也能做到。从 Louis XIV 时代一直到今天，你其实可以说，全球政治权力博弈的主线，就是这个英语海洋商业自由秩序的崛起，然后被一连串大陆强国先后挑战：Louis XIV 治下的 France，然后是 Napoleon，然后是德国、普鲁士在一战，以及——

turns.en: then World War II, the Soviet Union, and that these contests have been incredibly difficult. There have been moments in every case where the technocratic centralized land power looked like it was just walking away and the ridiculous confused commercial English-speaking maritime alliance was muddle lost, crazy, and yet somehow in the end, the hobbits keep winning.
turns.zh: ——然后是二战，然后是苏联。这些较量都艰难至极。每一次都有那么一些时刻，看起来那个技术官僚的中央集权陆权国家就要赢者通吃，而那个滑稽、混乱、做生意的英语海洋同盟已经一败涂地、疯成一团——然而不知为何，到最后，霍比特人总是在赢。

turns.en: I should say that we stole our global strategy from the British. They stole it from the Dutch who had been doing this earlier in the 17th century.
turns.zh: 我得说，我们的全球战略是从 British 那里偷来的，而 British 是从 Dutch 那里偷来的——Dutch 在 17 世纪更早就开始这么干了。

turns.en: In Dot and Gold, one of my books, I say that you could sum up the last 300 years of modern history in 10 letters, UP, United Provinces, to UK, to US.
turns.zh: 在我的一本著作（Dot and Gold）里，我说过去 300 年的现代历史可以用 10 个字母来概括：UP——United Provinces（联合省，即荷兰）——到 UK，再到 US。

turns.en: Now, obviously, that raises the question to question mark, question mark, question mark. I don't think China has it in it to beat us. What is that strategy, the maritime strategy?
turns.zh: 当然，这就引出了那个问题：接下来是问号、问号、问号。我不认为 China 有打败我们的那点东西。这个战略到底是什么——海洋战略？

turns.en: What are these three entities done that's been so effective to let the hobbits win? I don't know if I can really reveal all this, the secret five-point plan for global dominance.
turns.zh: 这三个实体到底做对了什么，才这么有效、让霍比特人总能赢？我不知道自己是不是真能把这一切都抖落出来——这份全球霸权的秘密五点计划。

turns.en: Okay, why not? Right, I'm just going to ask everyone who hears this to kind of be careful with how they use this information, be terrible if it fell into the wrong hands.
turns.zh: 好吧，为什么不呢？行，那我只恳请每一位听到这段节目的人谨慎使用这些信息，要是落进坏人手里可就糟了。

turns.en: Step one is have an open society at home. Think of the Dutch in the 17th century. Okay, everybody had these wars of religion. Well, the Dutch are pretty Calvinist, but they say, well, you know what, these Lutherans, they're scum, they're going to hell, everybody knows that.
turns.zh: 第一步，在国内建一个开放社会。想想 17 世纪的荷兰。当时大家都陷在宗教战争里。荷兰人很加尔文主义，但他们说：好吧，那些路德宗是渣滓、要下地狱，人尽皆知——

turns.en: But you know, until they do, they could kind of pay taxes and contribute to the economy. And even the Catholics, I mean, of course, they can't do their filthy idolaters' rights in the streets or anything.
turns.zh: ——但在真下地狱之前，他们总归能交税、能给经济做贡献。甚至天主教徒也一样——当然，他们那些偶像崇拜的仪式不能摆到街上来。

turns.en: But yeah, live and let live, the Jews live and let live. If an intellectual scientist publishes some kind of scientific paper that the church doesn't like, well, people will write nasty comments about it in other journals.
turns.zh: 但总体上就是 live and let live（相安无事），对犹太人也是 live and let live。如果某个学者或科学家发表了一篇教会不喜欢的科学论文，顶多是别人在别的期刊上写些刻薄的评论。

turns.en: But when Galileo doesn't go to the prison, there's no inquisition. And also, if you have an idea, you can try it. If you are the son of a peasant and you want to sort of try it as a merchant and you can find some people who let you do it, go right ahead.
turns.zh: 但 Galileo 不用下监狱，也没有宗教裁判所。而且如果你有想法，你就可以去试。如果你是农民的儿子，想试着做做生意，只要能找到愿意让你做的人，那就尽管去干。

turns.en: They come up with new ideas for government finance that we still use, the joint stock company, new seagoing technology, circulation of the blood, Locke comes to Holland and writes a lot of his best work there.
turns.zh: 他们想出许多我们今天还在沿用的政府财政新点子，发明了股份公司（joint stock company），搞出新的航海技术，有了血液循环（circulation of the blood）的研究，Locke 跑到荷兰，在那儿写出了他很多最好的作品。

turns.en: That's step one. You have this open dynamic society and you've got the intellectuals are flocking there, your universities are flourishing. Step two is now with all of these products that you've developed and innovative technology you take to show on the road, you trade globally.
turns.zh: 这是第一步。你有了这个开放而充满活力的社会，知识分子蜂拥而至，大学欣欣向荣。第二步是：现在把你研发的所有产品、所有创新技术拿到路上去展示，你要做全球贸易。

turns.en: So you have, I think there were 10,000 seagoing ships coming from the Netherlands in the 17th century and they're traveling all over the world.
turns.zh: 于是——我想 17 世纪从荷兰出发的远洋船有一万艘——它们航行到世界各地。

turns.en: And what this does is it makes you stinking rich. I advise my students sometimes to go to the Met Museum here or any number of places to see the Dutch masters, not to look for, oh, like the brushstrokes and the composition that's so exquisite, all of which is true.
turns.zh: 这么做的结果就是让你富得流油。我有时会建议学生去大都会博物馆（Met）或者别的地方看荷兰大师的画——不是去看『哎呀，笔触和构图多么精妙』，虽然这些确实都是真的。

turns.en: But just look at all the stuff that these people have in their painting. Here's the merchant with his silk robe from China and he's standing on a rug from Turkey and he's got a stuffed parrot from Brazil on his mental face.
turns.zh: 而是看画里这些人拥有的东西：这位商人穿着从中国来的丝绸长袍，脚下踩着土耳其的地毯，身边还摆着一只来自巴西的标本鹦鹉。

turns.en: There's just this astounding amount of wealth which then allows you to start thinking globally. 18th century, the Prussians fight, Frederick the Great fights with Maria Theresa over Silesia.
turns.zh: 画里是惊人的一笔财富，而财富让你开始用全球眼光思考。到了 18 世纪，普鲁士人开打了——Frederick the Great 和 Maria Theresa 在争夺 Silesia（西里西亚）。

turns.en: The Seven Years War, this is a beautiful, I've been there, I've been to Silesia, I love Silesia. It's a sausage shaped province in modern Poland and seven years, both countries go bankrupt and in the end, Frederick gets it, which means he's Frederick the Great and it's just Maria Theresa who lost.
turns.zh: 七年战争。那地方真美，我去过 Silesia，我爱 Silesia。它是今天 Poland 境内一条香肠形状的省。打了七年，双方都打破产了。最后是 Frederick 拿到了，于是成了『腓特烈大帝』，输的只是 Maria Theresa。

turns.en: But during that Seven Years War, the British basically kicked the French out of India and Canada and North America and established the foundations of the world order that we still live today.
turns.zh: 但在那场七年战争期间，British 基本把 French 赶出了 India、Canada 和北美，奠定了我们今天仍然身处其中的世界秩序的地基。

turns.en: So you're thinking globally. Once you have built this global system, you then do something extremely treacherous, which is you invite everyone else to participate in your system.
turns.zh: 所以你要用全球眼光思考。而一旦建成这个全球体系，你接下来要做一件极其冒险的事——邀请所有人来加入你的体系。

turns.en: So you don't have to say what the Spanish did in Latin America where you say, this is ours, we conquered this, nobody else can trade here, you people stay out, which obviously consents it to a certain stagnation.
turns.zh: 这样你就不必像 Spanish 在拉丁美洲那样——『这块是我们的，是我们打下来的，别的谁都不许来做买卖，都给我出去』——而那当然会让它陷入某种停滞。

turns.en: The British in the 19th century, they have free trade in the British Empire, everybody can trade and the British Navy keeps piracy down for everybody, not just for the Brits.
turns.zh: 19 世纪的 British 在大英帝国内搞自由贸易，谁都可以来做生意；而 British Navy 替所有人压制海盗，不只替 British 自己。

turns.en: And what this does is it encourages other countries to participate in your system. As we did with Britain, we didn't fight with them after 18, 12, we came close a couple of times, but at the end of the day, we traded in the British system.
turns.zh: 这样做的效果，是鼓励其他国家加入你的体系。我们对 Britain 就是这样：1812 年之后我们没再打过仗——中间差点打过几次——但终究，我们是在 Britain 的体系里做贸易。

turns.en: We were among the greatest beneficiaries of what the British did. And the Germans did the same thing, Prussia, the German Empire became a great trading power.
turns.zh: 我们是 what the British did 最大的受益者之一。Germans 也是一样：普鲁士、德意志帝国成了贸易大国。

turns.en: They had investments in Argentina and Chile, and in many places, their commerce was driving out the British. Then the Germans discovered that we have another little trick up our sleeves.
turns.zh: 他们在 Argentina 和 Chile 以及许多地方有投资，他们的商业在很多领域把 British 挤了出去。然后 Germans 发现：我们袖子里还藏着一招。

turns.en: They go to war in World War One, and they suddenly discover that while they were integrating into the world, that made them very rich, gave them great technology, a lot of military power, but now they're dependent on suddenly there are war with the UK and they can't get all that grain from Argentina and America that fed their people.
turns.zh: 他们打了一战，然后突然发现：融入世界的过程虽然让他们极富有、给了他们极好的技术和强大的军事力量，但他们也因此产生了依赖——忽然和 UK 开战，Argentina 和 America 那些养活他们国民的粮食就进不来了。

turns.en: They can't get that imported rubber from Malaya that provides the tires that they need for war. So they've grown dependent on that international system, and you're able to cut it off, and this is one of the big reasons the English won so many of these wars.
turns.zh: Malaya 进口的橡胶——战争所需的轮胎就靠它——也进不来了。所以他们越来越依赖那套国际体系，而你有能力把供应掐断，这就是 English 赢了这么多场战争的重要原因之一。

turns.en: So this system exists, I think a lot of Americans really aren't conscious of it, but we sort of revert to these patterns. Things happen and we just bathe in these ways.
turns.zh: 所以这套体系一直存在。我想很多美国人在意识层面并不清楚它，但我们的行为总会回到这些模式上来。事情一旦发生，我们本能地就用这些方式来应对。

turns.en: So after the end of the Cold War, what do we say to Russia and China? Come on in. And just as we said to Germany and Japan in 1945, benefit from the system.
turns.zh: 所以冷战结束后，我们对 Russia 和 China 说什么？『进来吧。』就像 1945 年对 Germany 和 Japan 说的：『来享受这个体系的好处吧。』

turns.en: Actually we waited about 47 to do that, but in any case, come on in, benefit. And now both Germany and Japan are principal pillars of the world system.
turns.zh: 其实我们等了大约 47 年才这么做，但无论如何，『进来吧，受益吧。』如今 Germany 和 Japan 都是世界体系的顶梁柱。

turns.en: We sort of hoped that Russia and China would do that too. We've taken more of the Wilhelm the second path than the Conrad Adenauer path. We are now testing what happens there.
turns.zh: 我们也曾希望 Russia 和 China 同样如此。但他们走的更接近 Wilhelm II 的路，而不是 Konrad Adenauer 的路。现在我们正在看这条路通向哪里。

turns.en: It's one of the reasons I'm worried, but it's a pattern that has been recurring, and so far whenever it finally comes to the test, our side has been winning.
turns.zh: 这是我担忧的原因之一。但这是一个一再重现的模式，而到目前为止，每当真到了考验关头，赢的总是我们这一边。

turns.zh: Ridgeline 是首个内置 AI 的端到端记录系统（system of record），投资管理公司在一个统一平台上完成组合核算、对账、报告、交易和合规。
